I always thought that was normal - indeed, I'm pretty sure it was until recently.  My interpretation of the advice is that it acknowledges two things:

1 There is a heightened risk of supply chains being disrupted - by natural or hostile action - and it might be three days or so before either things get back to normal or emergency measures take effect.  But mainly...

2 There are increasing numbers of people who don't keep supplies of essentials.  Some might not be able to afford to do so; but I suspect the advice is aimed mainly at people who think they'll always be able to order things delivered to them at the drop of a hat and therefore keep almost nothing in the house.

What scaremongering. I have fasted twice in my life: for 42 days in 2001 and for 75 days in 2023, both times in India. The first time I lost 10 kg; the second, 22 kg. Neither fast felt particularly difficult to me.
I drank purified water, took minerals and vitamins, and stayed active with daily exercise or long walks. After about a week, I no longer felt hungry.
The funny thing was that I kept my strength. As my weight dropped, moving became easier. I felt stronger every day and started taking the stairs two steps at a time instead of one.
After two months without food, I was still riding my scooter with a friend on the back. He filmed part of the trip. We were laughing and joking. I certainly did not feel as though I was about to collapse.
Our bodies store fat as an energy reserve. Mine finally had a chance to put that reserve to use.
That is why warnings that seem to suggest we fall apart after three days without food strike me as ridiculous. My own experience was very different.
Of course, my experience does not mean that such a long fast is safe for everyone, or that vitamins and minerals remove all the risks. But personal accounts belong in the discussion too. Read what people whohave actually fasted have to say, alongside the medical research.

“Britons are being told to stay at home because we’re preparing for war” is misleading.

I’ve checked the latest UK information because this is current news.

What is actually happening
The UK Government is preparing a new public information campaign encouraging households to keep some basic emergency supplies, including bottled water and long-life/tinned food. This has been reported in the UK over the last couple of days. 

But importantly:

There is no instruction for people in Britain to stay at home because war is imminent.

There has been no announcement telling people to go into lockdown or shelter at home.

The proposed advice is about being able to cope with a range of emergencies — things such as severe weather, flooding, power/infrastructure problems, cyber-attacks and hostile-state activity — rather than saying Britain is about to go to war. 

The Government's existing preparedness website already advises people to consider having water and non-perishable food available in case of an emergency. 

So where has the “war” story come from?
I think something has been lost in translation or sensationalised in the Italian reporting.

There genuinely is increased concern in the UK about national security, Russia, cyber-attacks and the possibility of major disruption. The Government's latest resilience report explicitly talks about the more complicated security environment and hostile-state activity. 

And British newspapers have reported that the Government is preparing advice along the lines of having three days of basic supplies at home.

But that's quite different from:

“The British are being told to stay at home because Britain is preparing for war.”

That is not what the current UK guidance says.

In fact, the official preparedness site describes this as preparing for emergencies generally, rather than telling the population that a war is about to happen. 

So I wouldn't panic at all based on your friend's message. She hasn't completely invented the story — there is a genuine new UK preparedness initiative — but the “stay at home / prepare for war” version makes it sound considerably more alarming than the actual British advice.

For an 'unlimited supply of candles', get an empty jar and fill it with used cooking oil. Then, add rock salt, making sure the oil level is higher than the salt.

Get a cotton bud and cut it in half. Dip the cotton end into the oil, then stick it in the middle of the jar until it stands upright, with the cotton part sticking out above the oil. Then, light it.

The measurements depend on the size of your jar, but you can use a 50 ml or 100 ml jar. You don't need to fill it completely. Just add enough rock salt to fill about 1/4 of the jar, then pour in the used cooking oil until it sits about half an inch above the salt.

This is what we used to do on the farm. One jar can last for a month or even longer.

Hint:  To build up supplies work towards -- First !!  All the foods that you use regularly, have one open and one unopened on the shelf.  Then !  Gradually build towards one open and two on the shelf.  Things you use more frequently have one open and three on the shelf !!  After that, start ensuring water supply (a camping barrel, for a water supply that you can roll from A to B holds about 40 litres -- get one of those, keep it full if you wish, or fill it when warnings are issued;  on a low budget, save those drinks and milk bottles.  Then get another  one, or two, of those barrels for waste !!  Get re-chargeable torches that clip onto metal surfaces with magnets, or hang from hooks !!  If you are getting really serious, you can have emergency lights installed (by an electrician) at a few points in the house that give a few hours background lighting automatically when the power goes off -- not good for days, but enough for preparations to be made, bags to be packed, extra blankets to be found, or to find the kayak in the garage to take you through the floodwaters !!! Prepping is really just being pragmatic. Living in a rural area with harsh winters it’s a reality that the power goes out, the roads close and supply chains break down. Having a store of water to drink and water to flush is just common sense. We currently have at least a years worth of food in our pantry. And less than 10 percent of that is from a store. We grow it, we harvest it and we preserve it. This is the seceond year we added meat chickens to our growing. Our growing and preserving (canning, fermenting and dehydrating) started out as a way to ensure the highest quality food, free of additives and heirloom varieties loaded with nutrients so often bred out of the food in stores. It also turns out to be enormously cheaper to grow your own food and takes much less space than people imagine. As climate has become more extreme, as world events have made life more dangerous in many places, our growing and preserving and plans for power/fuel shortages takes on another dimension. It’s not fear based, it’s simply risk management. As a project manager in the corporate world, every well run project has a risk plan. That includes identification of the risks, assessment of their likelihood and their impact should they happen. Based on the assessment each risk than has a mitigation plan that matches the risk profile. Prepping need not be selfish nor conspiracy driven. It can be simple risk and opportunity management. Asking yourself if you can have water and eat for 3 days is about as low level prep as one could imagine. We’ve seen storms where power was out for more than 3 days and roads were closed for a week. Last year, in a fairly normal winter the school had over 30 snow days. Initially when we started getting organized we ensured we have to heat sources in the house (electric and propane) as the risk of both being unavailable was pretty low. That risk is changing, just with weather and without considering other triggering factors. So now, being pragmatic, we are simply asking ourselves what option 3 needs to be. We are also exploring things like a manual well pump that can coexist with the electric well pump. It’s really not about fear or some belief in a massive military event but more about being pragmatic and doing things that will help us be safe, healthier and live cheaper. It’s also a recognition that if one of those black balls come out of the urn (we live an hour or so away from a major nuclear power plant) there is very little likelihood our ‘prepping’ will matter. That level of risk you simply have to make peace with.

Folks, being prepared was never some odd orientation being carried out by "preppers".  There are long traditions that had built in with it preparedness - having a cold cellar/root cellar.  Canning and pickling.  Storing wood or peat as winter fuel.  Preserving meats in salt and fat.  Having a store of grains or flour.  That was daily life for hundreds, if not thousands of years in old agrarian cultures.

Modern life has given us choice, distribution, and convenience - but that is all based on international supply chains that were always fragile.  We need to reintroduce some old practices back into our daily lives.  Have a cold room/storage room where you can place canned goods, pickled goods, pasta, rice, beans, and other dry goods you care to have.  You can have bottled water, or even wine stored on racks.  Dried meats such as jerky can be kept.  Powdered milk.  Powdered eggs. Sugar.  If you can manage, a portable bbq. or a portable butane hob with some canisters of butane.  You could have a small alcohol stove with methyl spirits.  Wax candles.

Other things - if you have a back garden - grow vegetables that you can preserve.  Camping equipment, is actually multi-purpose - not only for the act of camping, but also for outdoor entertaining and in emergencies (camping stoves and fuel, sleeping bags, mylar blankets, coolers, LED lights, head torches and more).

A spare car battery on a tender and an inverter can help in a short blackout - portable/foldable solar panels in longer emergencies.  Your tool batteries (Makita, deWalt, Bosch, and others) many have 5V inverters to power your devices.

Going on actual camping trips not only can be good fun, but they can serve as a "shake test" of the gear you have accumulated and refresh your memory on how to use some of that stuff.  The longer the trip you can go on comfortably, the better prepared you can be when certain services fail.  Incorporating tool batteries and a car battery with inverter is a great way to measure and gain insight into your person electrical energy consumption.

If you have a technical bent - get involved with amateur radio - get your license and you can also serve your local community by becoming back-up communications to your local municipal services.  For those not interested, some sort of radio would suffice that can be battery powered/recharged, or hand cranked.  You can even get what are called SDR dongles that can be driven by an ipad or phone to tune into stations both close and afar.

None of this needs to be done with an impending sense of doom.  It can all be done with family and friends, with neighbours, and within your community. Indeed if people all did this and incorporated traditions - both new and old - people and communities in general would be more resilient.  Camping trip outings reveal and test equipment and can build skill.  Amateur radio backs up communities and they have fun events that are also "shake tests" of communications.  Special potlucks can be held to use up older preserved foods to make way for newly preserved foods.  Group hikes with lunches cooked on portable stoves can bring people together, test equipment, use up older dried goods, and pass information with each other.

Nobody knows when the next crisis will come - but you can set things aside, preserve, test, connect, and build skill, all while having fun.  The best bit of all - these doing these activities and learning from them can actually ease any anxiety about the future, as you have actually done some preparedness.

You need a long term storage plan first.  See previous sentence.  You also need to be storing food based on when it must be used by.  Put the food in boxes and mark them by month/year to be eaten.  Then you must live on what you have stored to ensure your storage plan is healthy, edible, complete, and in sufficient quantity for the stored time period.  If not, you can make adjustments before its too late.  Dont just put a lot of food on shelves.  You will end up throwing most of that food in the garbage.  Plan it and then execute it.  Then keep on adding further food storage to extend the years of supply as you are using it.  Know the shelf life on every food so that it is stored in the correct year/month boxes.  Concentrate on buying and storing meats and fish.  Plan on growing your own vegetables and fruit.  Canning and freeze drying are excellent for long term storage.  Dont store food in their original packages.  Use mylar bags, jars, and large metal cans with lids, dont want rodents and insects infecting your food.  Keep in a cool dry place.  Dont buy food stuffs that are difficult, time consuming, or costly in energy to prepare.  Get rid of the food that you are used to and do research on what foods provide the most nutrition.  You need to get used to eating those foods now.  Eat organic, and check the ingredients of what you buy.  Plan ahead, adjust plan as needed, and keep extending your supply.

The reality in Latvia (from the Latvian perspective) is this - until the war in Ukraine, 90% of the Latvian population tolerated Russian culture in every single way. We had Russian media, Russian schools, Russian monuments, Russian events, etc. No matter where you went, to a club, restaurant, or any other place - you could easily communicate in Russian. 

After the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2021, things have changed. We removed most USSR monuments, prohibited most of the Russian TV channels, removed the Russian language from street signs, and restaurant menus, we are refusing to buy Russian gas or oil from now on, etc. There will be no Russian schools or kindergartens - in every educational institution in Latvia, the Latvian language will be the primary from now on.

Some people would say it is wrong, it is Russophobic, etc. But you have to understand that we as an independent country have the rights to shape our internal culture as we want and consider correct. Those who want to stay can adopt. Those who don`t like it can leave. 

It doesn`t mean we have physical aggression against Russians. No. We are just saying that because of what happened in Ukraine, we are finally making some changes that we have been putting off since the collapse of the USSR.

Para todos los que dicen, "¿y por que juegos? ¡que estupida recomendación! acaso debajo de los escombros me voy a poner a jugar" les digo, La mochila de 72 horas no está pensada para el minuto exacto en que te cae un escombro encima — para eso lo que salva es un casco, no un parqués. Está pensada para los días DESPUÉS: cuando ya saliste, tu casa quedó inhabitable, y te tocó esperar 3, 5, 7 días en un albergue o carpa con tus hijos sin nada que hacer más que ver el desastre a tu alrededor.
Ahí es exactamente donde entra lo que mencionó el experto, y no es capricho: FEMA (la agencia oficial de manejo de emergencias de EE.UU.) recomienda explícitamente incluir "libros, juegos, rompecabezas u otras actividades para los niños" (Ready.gov) dentro del kit básico de emergencia. No lo inventó un youtuber, lo dice el organismo que literalmente escribe el manual de qué llevar en un desastre.
Y no es solo por "entretener". Organismos humanitarios como UNICEF y Save the Children implementan lo que se llama "espacios amigables para la niñez" en zonas de desastre, con juegos y actividades estructuradas, porque el juego regula el estrés agudo, le da a un niño (y honestamente a un adulto también) una sensación de normalidad y control en medio del caos, y reduce síntomas de ansiedad y trauma en los días posteriores al evento. Esto es un pilar reconocido dentro de los protocolos de Primeros Auxilios Psicológicos que usa la Red Nacional de Estrés Traumático Infantil (NCTSN) en EE.UU.
Entonces no, nadie va a sacar el parqués debajo de una viga. Pero si tu familia va a pasar días esperando ayuda con los nervios en el piso, un mazo de cartas pesa 50 gramos y puede ser la diferencia entre un niño que se desregula emocionalmente y uno que aguanta mejor la espera. Eso no es ignorancia del experto, es que hay gente que solo entiende "supervivencia" como la película y no como lo que realmente es: sostener a tu familia física Y mentalmente hasta que llegue la ayuda.
